title: Kubernetes example manifests
description: Serves "Installing is boring.". Example manifests an operator applies with kubectl: deployments per role, readiness and liveness, Postgres (CNPG), configuration as plain files. Split from the Helm chart (JS-142) by the direction review, 2026-11-19: an operator cannot install jellyscale today.
acceptanceCriteria: Example manifests in the repository install jellyscale on a fresh cluster with kubectl alone (`kubectl apply -k` or `-f`), no Helm

Readiness and liveness probes per role. Each probe states what it depends on: liveness never depends on Postgres or a store, so a database failover restarts no pod; ffmpeg threads follow the pod's CPU limit, not the node's cores

The manifests size CNPG's max_connections from their own configuration: every process's databaseMaxConns plus the direct connections each worker holds (liveness, lease keeper, and one per running scan, segment sweep or asset sweep pass), with headroom; configuration whose sum exceeds it is refused by a check
The worker's liveness URL can come from the environment or a Secret, and the manifests never put a password in a process's arguments
docs/running.md says which Postgres connection modes are supported (session; a transaction-mode pooler or pgx exec mode, supported or not, by a check), and the manifests connect that way
A replica whose database stays broken leaves service, and the manifests' grace period and readiness lead match the documented ones

The example manifests declare trustedProxies for their ingress (D-020) The procedure in docs/running.md for confirming declared proxies, followed against the example manifests' ingress, says what the operator sees and does when no address is counted (every answer 401, no refusal line), and no sentence there denies a log line the server writes (D-025, BL-221)

Workers are their own Deployment, apart from api and stream, and the manifests' check refuses more than one worker or stream replica on a transcode store or library that not every one of them can reach (a ReadWriteOnce volume), naming the key (D-045) docs/running.md says what every worker must reach (Postgres, each library, the transcode store), and the worker's termination grace matches JS-165's (D-045) The example manifests declare no transcodeCores and give workers CPU requests equal to limits in whole cores (D-064)
notes: JS-020 (2026-11-08): each worker holds one Postgres connection for its liveness lock, outside the pool, so a stock Postgres (max_connections 100) is exhausted at about 90 workers, long before its CPU (one primary carried 1600 streams on two cores' worth). Connections are the first wall when autoscaling. User (2026-11-08): plain manifests for kubectl are wanted beside the chart, not Helm only. JS-166 (D-067): its docs/running.md part was not written and is carried by criteria 10 and 11 here and JS-177's 'Sizing workers'. From its record, criterion 11's text covers: every role given the same transcodeStore and its S3 credentials; and that a request equal to the limit may not schedule beside a node's other workloads (the dogfood's worker requests 6 under a limit of 12), which is why a 4K-capable worker wants a whole node. D-069: each 'by a check' in criteria 3, 6 and 10 is met by the application refusing or warning at start with the key named, or by the shipped manifests applied to a real cluster in this task's own run; no test reads the manifest files. A criterion that cannot be met that way returns as a brief when the task starts. D-071: the example worker's CPU limit is one the docs' rules hold for (a 2-CPU limit counts 2.0, under the 4K HDR job's 2.08 share). The example configuration names no `transcodeSlots`; whether that key is removed or capped at the CPUs returns as a brief at Refine.
